blogs.title: From ‘Right to Control’ to Fraudulent Inducement: How the Fifth Circuit Reframed Pump-and-Dump Liability After Ciminelli and Kousisis
blogs.description: This post would examine the opinion’s central doctrinal move: distinguishing the barred right-to-control theory from a valid fraudulent-inducement theory. It would explain why the Fifth Circuit treated social-media misstatements as allegations that investors were tricked into parting with money, not merely deprived of useful market information, and assess how the court used Kousisis to preserve federal fraud prosecutions after Ciminelli. The post would also explore whether this framing meaningfully narrows fraud law or instead gives prosecutors a ready path around Ciminelli in securities cases.

blogs.title: Must Securities Fraud Aim to Harm Investors? The Fifth Circuit Says No—and That Matters
blogs.description: This post would focus on the court’s treatment of intent to defraud. Relying on Kousisis, the panel held that the government need not allege that defendants sought to leave victims economically worse off; it is enough that defendants sought to obtain money by materially false pretenses. The post would analyze the implications of divorcing fraud from net pecuniary harm, especially in market transactions where victims receive something of facially equivalent value, and consider whether this approach expands criminal exposure in modern trading and promotional practices.

blogs.title: Section 1348 as Mail-and-Wire Fraud in Securities Clothing: The Fifth Circuit’s Borrowing Problem
blogs.description: This post would analyze the court’s methodological choice to interpret 18 U.S.C. § 1348 through mail- and wire-fraud doctrine. Because Fifth Circuit precedent on § 1348 is sparse, the panel imported concepts like ‘scheme to defraud,’ ‘intent to defraud,’ and property-based limitations from general fraud cases. The post would consider the benefits and risks of this cross-pollination: whether it promotes coherence across fraud statutes, or whether it obscures securities-law-specific concerns such as market manipulation, investor protection, and the distinct role of deception in securities markets.

blogs.title: Finfluencers, Criminal Fraud, and the Future of Market Manipulation Cases
blogs.description: This post would place the case in a broader enforcement context, highlighting how traditional fraud doctrine is being applied to social-media-driven trading schemes. It would discuss what the opinion signals for criminal cases against online stock promoters, the evidentiary importance of allegations about secret selling and false statements about trading positions, and the likely boundaries between lawful touting, reckless hype, and criminal manipulation. The post would be especially useful for practitioners advising clients in the rapidly developing area of influencer-based securities promotion.
